name: CMT type 1B (MPZ)
aliases: hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type IB

clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant demyelinating neuropathy caused by variants in the myelin protein zero (MPZ) gene, which encodes the principal structural protein of compact peripheral myelin
Presents like classic CMT with distal wasting, pes cavus, hammer toes, foot drop, absent ankle reflexes and glove-and-stocking sensory loss, though onset ranges from infancy to late adulthood
Phenotype is strikingly variable: some patients have early severe demyelinating disease resembling Dejerine-Sottas, others a later-onset milder axonal picture
Nerve conduction studies typically show markedly and uniformly slowed motor conduction velocities, reflecting the diffuse demyelinating process
Pupillary abnormalities such as Adie-like tonic pupils and prominent sensory features can be clues pointing towards an MPZ cause
Diagnosis rests on characteristic clinical and electrophysiological findings confirmed by identification of a pathogenic MPZ variant
Management is supportive: ankle-foot orthoses, physiotherapy, foot surgery for deformity and avoidance of neurotoxic agents
reference.pathophysiology: The MPZ gene encodes myelin protein zero, the dominant adhesion protein of compact myelin in the peripheral nerves, where it holds adjacent myelin lamellae together. Pathogenic variants disrupt myelin compaction and Schwann cell function, producing either a dominant-negative or a gain-of-function effect depending on the variant. Some mutations cause early, severe dysmyelination presenting in infancy, while others allow relatively normal early myelination followed by a later axonal degeneration. The resulting segmental demyelination and remyelination slow saltatory conduction and, over time, lead to secondary axonal loss that underlies the fixed weakness and sensory deficit.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies to demonstrate uniform slowing of motor conduction velocities
Targeted MPZ sequencing or a hereditary neuropathy gene panel
Detailed family history and examination of relatives for subclinical disease
Sural nerve biopsy in atypical cases, showing onion-bulb formation and demyelination
Serum protein electrophoresis and inflammatory markers to exclude acquired demyelinating causes
Ophthalmological review where pupillary abnormalities are suspected
redFlags: Rapid subacute deterioration suggesting a superimposed acquired inflammatory neuropathy rather than pure inherited disease
Severe infantile hypotonia and respiratory compromise from a Dejerine-Sottas-like MPZ phenotype
Prominent proximal weakness or sensory ataxia disproportionate to the length-dependent pattern
New bulbar or breathing difficulty requiring urgent assessment
reference.prognosis: Course depends heavily on the specific variant; many patients have a slowly progressive disability compatible with independent walking into later life, whereas early-onset severe forms cause substantial childhood disability. Life expectancy is generally normal.
pitfalls: Mislabelling a treatable acquired demyelinating neuropathy as inherited disease and withholding immunotherapy
Assuming a single genotype-phenotype rule when MPZ variants span demyelinating to axonal presentations
Overlooking family members with mild or subclinical disease
Prescribing potentially neurotoxic drugs without considering the underlying neuropathy
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Manage supportively, as no disease-modifying therapy exists, with physiotherapy to preserve strength, balance and joint range
Fit ankle-foot orthoses for foot drop and provide podiatry and appropriate footwear for pes cavus and hammer toes
Consider orthopaedic foot surgery such as tendon transfer or arthrodesis for fixed, disabling deformity
Treat neuropathic pain and cramps symptomatically and avoid potentially neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine
Screen for the MPZ-associated features of tonic (Adie-like) pupils and sensorineural hearing loss with ophthalmology and audiology review
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance, using the strong genotype-phenotype correlation to inform prognosis, and assess at-risk relatives
Coordinate multidisciplinary neuromuscular, orthopaedic and rehabilitation care
